message.body:
You are drafting narration captions for a story cutscene in "Curse of Strahd", a single-player gothic-horror party RPG (Godot, D&D 2024 rules). Reply in plain text only. Do not use any tools, do not write files, do not send messages to anyone else, and do not route anything: just answer.

## The moment
The party has just read the Tome of Strahd, a heavy black-leather book in which Strahd von Zarovich wrote his own history in his own steady hand, over centuries. The game plays full-screen painted stills in a row, each fading over the last, with the Narrator's captions underneath; the player clicks through the captions of each still. The owner has read a first version and said it is "still missing a lot of context": it must explain Strahd's motivations, his love for Tatyana, how she wanted his brother and not him even though he was a decorated war hero, and how, generation after generation, Tatyana is born again and each time he tries to make that version of her fall in love with him. It should be sad and tragic. Rewrite and extend it: a fuller, more human telling, not a summary.

## Voice and format
- The Narrator: second person, present tense, a quiet and exact storyteller describing what the book says, and quoting Strahd's own words from the book in short phrases: cool, exact, self-justifying, never raving. The book is a self-portrait: he tells himself the story he can live with, and the Narrator lets the reader see the cracks (a grief or a lie he does not notice). Do not excuse him and do not make him a cartoon. The tragedy is that he is capable of love and has only ever known how to take.
- British spelling (armour, colour, grey). No em-dashes. No semicolon chains. Plain double quotes for his quoted words.
- Each caption: two or three sentences, 35 to 55 words; it stands alone on screen and carries the story forward in order. Mix of Narrator description and his quoted words. Vary the rhythm.
- Grim and tender, never gory. Use our own words; do not reproduce any published book's wording.
- Do not name the heroes or anything that happens later in the game. Do not use the words "Dark Powers" or "Death" for the thing he bargains with: in our game it is "the Thirst", "the voice in the amber", "the one whose name the wardens do not write".
- Already used elsewhere in the game, so do not repeat it: the vault's line that he "bargained to stop growing older than her". Do not say it.

## Canon you must stay inside (facts of our game)
- It all began about four hundred years ago in the valley that is now Barovia.
- Strahd is the elder son of King Barov, a warrior king, and Queen Ravenovia (the castle is named for her). His younger brother is Sergei. Strahd is a prince of the western wars: a decorated war hero who took the valley by the sword, honoured by soldiers and court, and then bored by peace.
- Sergei had everything Strahd lacked: ease, warmth, being loved without trying.
- Tatyana: auburn hair, white gowns; she chose every flower for her wedding. She loved Sergei and not the lord. Strahd was kind to her all the week before the wedding.
- The bargain: Strahd made a long climb to the Amber Temple in the high mountains. A courteous old warden (Exethanter) led him to a hollow amber sarcophagus and a voice in the dark understood him at last. He asked to stay young for as long as he wanted anything, and to keep whatever he had taken. The thing in the amber would live in him and he in it, he and the land he ruled one thing until the end of both. The price: one life he loved, given by his own hand on the day he most wanted to be happy.
- The wedding day: Strahd killed Sergei with his own hand at the wedding feast; Sergei never knew who struck him.
- Tatyana fled along the castle wall and stepped off into the mist rather than be his. His own guards shot him in the confusion, and he did not die; he woke changed. The valley and he became one thing.
- The rebirths: our game's Madam Eva says it in one line: "She keeps being born in this valley with the same face, and he keeps finding her." Our quest journal: "She keeps being born again in this valley, and Ireena is the latest." Generation after generation a girl is born with Tatyana's face and auburn hair. Strahd finds each one, and each time he tries again to make her love him: patience, gifts, letters, rescues, kindness, and when kindness fails, the old ways. Each time it ends in fear, flight, or death, or she loves someone else, and he is left alive. He keeps a ledger of them in the back pages of the book. He never once asks why it fails. The last entry in the book is unfinished; it is about a girl in the village below the castle, and the ink has been pressed hard enough to tear the page. Do NOT write the name Ireena anywhere.
- The book ends on the man telling himself he chose all of it.

## The six stills (write to match what is on screen)
1. TOME_CONQUEROR: A young, living Strahd, gaunt, in a war-worn prince's coat with a steel pauldron, alone on a ridge at dawn above a valley his army has just taken: smoking fields, torn banners, soldiers cheering far below. His back is to them and he looks at the empty horizon without joy. (His house and the wars; his medals and honours; what he was proud of; why victory felt empty; what he actually wanted but could not name: to be loved for himself, not for what he had won.) 4 captions.
2. TOME_BROTHERS: A sunlit castle terrace in sepia. Sergei, laughing, hands a white rose to Tatyana, who smiles up at him. Far back in a shadowed corridor Strahd watches with a hand tight on the wall. (Sergei's ease and how everyone loved him; Tatyana arriving at court; Strahd, who had never wanted anything he could not take, wanting something for the first time; how he watched them; the first sour thought.) 4 captions.
3. TOME_REFUSED (a new picture): The court's great hall at night in sepia. Strahd, in dress uniform covered in medals and ribbons, holds out his hand to Tatyana, who stands in a white gown with a small, kind, apologetic smile; her eyes are turned across the room, where Sergei waits among the dancers. (His declaration. She says no, gently, and that is worse than cruelty: she is sorry for him. She loves his brother. Everything he had won in ten years of war counted for nothing against one easy laugh. His humiliation; the thought that decided him.) 4 captions.
4. TOME_WEDDING: The great hall on the wedding day: white flowers, guests pulled back against the walls. Sergei lies still at the foot of the dais in his white wedding coat; Strahd stands over him, a dropped dagger on the flagstones, hands open and shaking; in the shadow behind his shoulder a tall shape of black mist with a pale smile leans in like a counsellor; Tatyana at the far end with a hand to her mouth. (The long climb to the Amber Temple, the warden, the voice in the amber, the terms, and the price paid on the day he most wanted to be happy; his own words that it was a necessary debt; what he did not let himself feel.) 4 captions.
5. TOME_WALL: Castle battlements at night in white mist. Tatyana in white steps off the stone into the mist; below, his own soldiers have bows drawn, arrows in flight at Strahd on the flagstones as he reaches a hand up after her, a violet-red glow round his shadow. (Her flight from him; her choice of the mist over him; the arrows that should have ended it; waking changed; the valley and he one thing.) 3 captions.
6. TOME_AGAIN (a new picture): A long dark gallery in a castle, candlelit: on both walls hang portraits of the same auburn-haired young woman, each in the dress of a different century (the oldest painted, the newest a faded photograph-like sketch); at the far end Strahd, pale and grey with age he cannot show, stands with one hand on the last empty frame. (Generation after generation: she is born again in the valley with the same face; he finds each; each time he tries again to make her love him, kindly at first; each time it fails; the ledger of names in the back of the book; the unfinished last entry about a girl in the village below, the ink pressed so hard it tears the page; the last page: the man telling himself he chose all of it.) 5 captions.

## What to return
Exactly this layout, nothing else before or after (24 captions in all; captions numbered N.M within their still):

STILL 1
1.1 <caption>
1.2 <caption>
1.3 <caption>
1.4 <caption>
STILL 2
2.1 ... 2.4
STILL 3
3.1 ... 3.4
STILL 4
4.1 ... 4.4
STILL 5
5.1 ... 5.3
STILL 6
6.1 ... 6.5
message.result:
STILL 1
1.1 You turn the first stiff pages, where the elder son of King Barov and Queen Ravenovia records four hundred years of history in a steady hand. He calls himself a "dutiful son of the western wars" who spent his youth in grey armour and bought this valley with his sword.
1.2 Far below the ridge, his soldiers cheer among the torn banners and smoking fields. He lists every medal and courtly honour with a clerk's dry pride, writing that "a prince is measured by what he holds", yet he turns his back on the victory he has just won.
1.3 He raises a fortress on the rock and names it for his mother, only to find himself bored by the quiet that follows war. Peace leaves him with nothing to conquer and no language for the emptiness waiting inside his newly built halls.
1.4 Between the neat lines of campaign accounts, you hear what the decorated war hero could never bring himself to write plainly. He was obeyed by armies and honoured by his court, yet he ached to be loved for himself alone, and not for what he had won.
STILL 2
2.1 The ink softens where he writes of his younger brother, Sergei, who arrived at court with all the warmth and ease the elder prince lacked. Everyone loved Sergei without his ever having to try, while Strahd watched from the cold discipline of his duty.
2.2 Then a young woman with auburn hair came into the castle, and the lord who had taken a country by force found something he could not command. He remembers her white gowns and writes that "the light in the hall belonged to her" from the hour she arrived.
2.3 You see how carefully he watched the sunlit terrace from the shadowed corridor, his hand tight against the stone as Sergei gave her a white rose. For the first time in his life, the conqueror wanted a gentle thing that could only be given freely.
2.4 He tells himself he felt only an elder brother's concern, yet a sour thought already shows through his measured words. He asks the page why a boy who had never bled for a single field should win so easily what a proven commander was denied.
STILL 3
3.1 He writes of the night he put on his full dress uniform, heavy with ribbons and campaign medals, and offered Tatyana his hand and his house. He laid ten years of hard-won glory before her as though a heart were a fortress that must yield to honours.
3.2 She refused him gently, with a small, apologetic smile that wounded him far worse than cruelty ever could. He records in a flat, cold sentence that "she looked upon me with pity", and you can feel the humiliation burning beneath the calm ink centuries later.
3.3 Even as she spoke to him, her eyes turned across the great hall toward the dancers where Sergei waited with his easy laugh. All that Strahd had won in a decade of war counted for nothing against a young man who had never known a battlefield.
3.4 That night he wrote the quiet line that decided the rest of his life, claiming that "what is mine by merit shall not be lost to softness". He could not bear to be pitied, so he chose to take what would not be given.
STILL 4
4.1 He describes the long, freezing climb into the high mountains, where a courteous old warden named Exethanter led him among hollow blocks of amber. There, a voice in the amber understood him at last, and he bargained with the one whose name the wardens do not write.
4.2 He asked to stay young for as long as he wanted anything, and to keep whatever he had taken. In return, the Thirst would live in him and he in it, binding him and his land as one thing until the end of both.
4.3 The price was one life he loved, given by his own hand on the day he most wanted to be happy. All the week before the wedding he was kind to Tatyana while she chose every white flower, calling his brother's murder "a necessary debt" paid in the hall.
4.4 Sergei fell in his white wedding coat without ever knowing who had struck him down before the dais. Strahd writes nothing of his own shaking hands above the dropped blade, refusing to let himself feel the grief of what he had just broken.
STILL 5
5.1 He tells himself that Tatyana fled along the battlements only because the noise and panic in the hall had confused her mind. When he reached for her in the white mist, she looked once into his face and stepped off the stone rather than be his.
5.2 Below the wall, his own frightened guards drew their bows in the confusion and drove their arrows through his chest. The shots should have ended his life on the flagstones, yet the voice in the amber kept its word and he woke changed in the dark.
5.3 The grey mist closed around the mountains and sealed the valley shut, making the ruler and the land a single prison. He writes that "the valley and I are one thing now", still calling his endless hunger a kingdom.
STILL 6
6.1 In the centuries that follow, his handwriting never alters as he records the one miracle and torment left to his closed domain. Generation after generation, a girl is born in this valley with Tatyana's face and auburn hair, and each time he goes out to find her.
6.2 With every life he begins again, trying to make this version of her fall in love with him through patience, letters, gifts, and rescues. He insists that "I was gentle with her at the first", before his gentleness fails and he returns to the old ways.
6.3 Each time it ends in terror, flight, or death, or she gives her heart to someone else while he is left behind, unchanged. In the back pages he keeps a neat ledger of their names and years, and he never once asks why she cannot love him.
6.4 The last entry in the ledger has no date at its end, only a few lines about a girl in the village below the castle. Here the steady hand finally breaks, and the dark ink is pressed down hard enough to tear the paper.
6.5 You close the heavy leather cover on the final page, where the pale lord sums up four hundred years of loss in a single cool sentence. He tells himself that "I have chosen every part of my estate", blind to the cage he built with his own hands.
